description_full: RPM International Inc. provides specialty chemicals for the construction, industrial, specialty, and consumer markets. It operates through CPG, PCG, and Consumer segments. The company offers waterproofing, coating, and traditional roofing systems; sealants, air barriers, tapes, and foams; residential home weatherization systems; roofing, and building maintenance services; sealing and bonding, subfloor preparation, glazing solutions; resin flooring systems, terrazzo, polyurethane, MMA waterproof, epoxy floor paint and coatings, concrete repair, and protection products, traffic deck coatings, and decorative concrete; fire stopping and intumescent coatings, and adhesive and sealant solutions; and rolled asphalt roofing materials and chemical admixtures. It also provides concrete and masonry admixtures, concrete fibers, cement grinding aids, cement performance enhancers, curing and sealing compounds, structural grouts and mortars, epoxy adhesives, polyurethane foams, floor hardeners and toppings, joint fillers, industrial and architectural coatings, decorative color/stains/stamps, restoration materials, insulated building cladding materials, specialty finishes, metal and composite materials, and exterior insulating and finishing systems; insulated concrete form and industrial concrete panel wall, engineered buck framing, and ICF bracing systems; and firestopping, flooring systems, weatherproofing solutions, and restoration services equipment. In addition, it offers corrosion control, fireproofing, edible, and factory applied industrial coatings; infrastructure repair and raised-flooring systems, fiberglass reinforced plastic structures, preservation products, specialty glazes, and food industry coatings; and rust-preventative, special purpose, and decorative paints, caulks, sealants, primers, contact cement, cleaners, woodcare coatings, abrasives, colorant, and other consumer products. The company was incorporated in 1947 and is headquartered in Medina, Ohio.

financial_summary: RPM International Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $13.2B market cap on $7.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 8% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 41%.

The business throws off $675M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.36× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.8×.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Carries a 53% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: 39 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (10%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.95x).
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $106.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 23% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $102 (margin of safety -1%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 19%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $77.48 to $137 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: EV/EBITDA 12.9 vs 8.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 18% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $124 on average, 20% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.4%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.21).
It runs a 41% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.36x.
ROE of 20% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.9x net debt to EBITDA ($318.4M of cash against $2.5B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.8x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.7% over 3 years, 5.2% over 5 years and 5.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 2.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.3%, and institutions hold 88%.
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (0.6% in buybacks and 2.2% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 6.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 17,500 employees, each generates about $449K of revenue, 0.7x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 5.8% a year.
That works out to $39K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
